subject: Communication
title: Ownership Bias: Who Owns the News?
description: Learn Ownership Bias: Who Owns the News? in one minute.

hook.text: Six corporations control 90% of American media. When your news company has a parent company, whose story gets told?

buildup.text: Media ownership consolidation means fewer independent voices. In 1983, fifty companies owned most US media — today, just six do.

discovery.text: Sinclair Broadcasting required 200+ local TV stations to air identical conservative commentary — disguised as local.

twist.text: Billionaire-owned media (Bezos/Washington Post, Murdoch/Fox) introduces different biases — not necessarily political.

climax.text: Media literacy requires knowing who owns what you consume. Ownership shapes editorial decisions, even when journalists resist.

punchline.text: Before you trust a story, check who's paying the storyteller.

quiz.question: How much of American media do six corporations control?

details.summary: Media ownership concentration means a handful of corporations control most news outlets. This creates structural bias not through direct editorial orders but through shared corporate interests, cost-cutting that reduces investigative capacity, and reluctance to challenge advertisers.
details.whyItMatters: Knowing who owns your news sources helps you understand what structural pressures shape their coverage and what stories they might avoid.
takeaways: A few corporations control most mainstream news outlets
Ownership creates structural bias, not direct editorial control
Corporate interests and advertiser relationships shape coverage

faq.question: How many companies control most of the media in the US?
faq.answer: As of recent counts, approximately six major corporations control the majority of mainstream US media. This has declined from about fifty companies in the 1980s. The specific companies shift through mergers and acquisitions, but the trend toward concentration continues.

faq.question: Does ownership actually affect news content?
faq.answer: Research consistently shows it does, though not through crude editorial dictates. Owned outlets tend to avoid stories that damage the parent company, favor deregulation, and reduce coverage of labor issues. The effect is subtle but measurable across large samples of coverage.
